title: What is actually inside a language model
lede: The whole argument in one sitting. This paper is about a specific reason a trained transformer has been so hard to read — the components the architecture hands you are not the components it computes in — and about a way to recover the second set from the first. The method is simple enough to state in a paragraph. What it turns up inside an MLP layer only 512 neurons wide is not simple at all.

beats.heading: The plan, and the component the architecture hands you
beats.body:
Start with the ordinary situation. You have a trained transformer. It works. You would like to know what it is doing — not statistically, but mechanically: which parts do what, and how the parts fit together.

The plan almost writes itself. Break the model into components. Work out what each component does. Work out how they compose. That is how you come to understand any other complicated machine.

So you need components, and the architecture offers an obvious one: the neuron. A single dimension of the MLP's hidden layer — one number per token, recomputed as the text flows past. You do not have to invent it, and it is not an arbitrary choice either: the non-linearity acts on exactly these numbers, one at a time, which is what makes them a natural place to look.

The model in this paper is deliberately small. One attention block, one MLP block, a [[residual-stream|residual stream]] 128 wide — the running vector each block reads from and writes back into — and an MLP hidden layer of 512 neurons, trained on 100 billion tokens of [[pile-dataset|the Pile]]. Those 512 numbers are what has to be read.

beats.heading: You look at one, and what comes back is a list
beats.body:
Take a neuron and find the text that makes it fire hardest. Collect the top examples and look for the pattern.

On this model it fails immediately. One neuron responds to academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests, and Korean text.

Not a concept. A list. This is [[polysemanticity]] — one unit, several unrelated meanings, and no principle joining them. It is not rare, and it is not confined to language models: the standard example from vision is a neuron in Inception v1 that fires on cat faces and on the fronts of cars.

It is worth pausing on why this is worse than it first sounds. The problem is not that the neuron is hard to describe. The problem is that it cannot be described *on its own*. Knowing it fired tells you one of four unrelated things is happening, and to find out which, you have to consult the other 511. The component has no meaning independent of its context — which is exactly the property that made components worth having. Every version of [[curse-of-dimensionality-in-interpretability|the difficulty of reading a large model]] descends from that.

And you cannot go around it. There are transformers you can analyse without ever touching hidden activations — the authors did exactly that for attention-only models in earlier work — but they are the ones with no MLP. Put a ReLU in the middle and the activation vector becomes something you have to face. A one-layer transformer with a single MLP block is, in their phrase, the simplest language model we profoundly do not understand.

beats.heading: Features are directions, and there are more of them than there are dimensions
beats.body:
Here is the hypothesis that makes sense of the mess, and it comes in two parts.

First, suppose the meaningful units are not neurons but *directions* in the 512-dimensional activation space — arbitrary mixtures, most of which do not line up with any axis. Each such direction is a [[feature]], and the claim that meaning lives in directions rather than in basis dimensions is the [[linear-representation-hypothesis]]. Sometimes a direction happens to coincide with an axis, and then you get a readable neuron and everyone is pleased. There is no reason it generally should.

Second, suppose the model has *more* of these directions than it has dimensions to give them. That is [[superposition]], and it sounds impossible for the obvious reason: 512 dimensions admit exactly 512 mutually perpendicular directions.

Two facts make it work anyway.

High-dimensional spaces are more spacious than they look. If you will accept *nearly* perpendicular instead of exactly, the number of directions you can pack in is not 512 but astronomically larger. Interference between any two exists; it is just small.

And the features are sparse. On any given token only a handful are active at all. Two directions that are not quite perpendicular only interfere when both are switched on, and mostly they are not. The interference stays under the threshold where it would change anything, and the ReLU takes care of much of the rest. This is why sparsity is not a pleasant extra property here but the load-bearing one — it is what makes the crowding survivable.

Put those together and the layer is doing something strange: a small dense network running a [[noisy-simulation]] of a much larger, much sparser one.

And now the neuron makes sense. If thousands of feature directions are scattered through 512 dimensions, every single axis has non-zero overlap with hundreds of them. Reading one neuron means reading hundreds of features at once, projected onto a line. Citations, dialogue, HTTP and Korean were never a meaning. They were a cross-section.

beats.heading: The obvious fix fails, and the loss function is the reason
beats.body:
If crowding is what breaks the neurons, uncrowd the model. Train it with heavy pressure toward sparse activations — in the limit, force one neuron active at a time. Accept worse loss in exchange for a readable model.

The authors [[activation-sparsity-training|spent real time on this]] and reached a conclusion stronger than “too expensive”. It is not viable, because you can eliminate superposition entirely and the neurons are *still* polysemantic.

The argument fits in a paragraph. Take one neuron that is either on or off, and four mutually exclusive, equally likely features in the data, each of which fully determines the next token.

If the neuron commits to feature A alone and predicts token A perfectly, then three quarters of the time it is silent, the model knows only “not A”, and it spreads its guess evenly over B, C and D. Under cross-entropy that costs about **0.82**.

If instead it fires on A *and* B and predicts a 50/50 blend, then when it fires the field is down to two, and when it is silent the field is down to the other two. That costs **ln 2 ≈ 0.69**.

Lower is better, so the polysemantic strategy wins — with a single neuron, in a setting where superposition is not even possible.

The reason sits in the objective. Cross-entropy rewards the probability you assigned to what actually came next, so being half-right about two things beats being certain about one and ignorant of three. No architectural change removes that incentive, because the incentive is in the loss. [[mse-loss-and-monosemanticity|Train under squared error instead]] and the pull disappears — but language models are not trained under squared error.

So the model is going to be polysemantic. Leave it alone and decompose its activations afterwards.

beats.heading: Dictionary learning, and a deliberately weak tool for it
beats.body:
Written as an equation, the hypothesis is that the activation vector at token *j* is approximately a bias plus a sparse weighted sum of unit vectors: `x ≈ b + Σᵢ fᵢ(x)·dᵢ`, with more directions `dᵢ` than the 512 dimensions they live in, and almost every coefficient `fᵢ` exactly zero.

That is not a new object. It is a linear matrix factorisation — the classic problem of [[dictionary-learning|sparse dictionary learning]], where the `dᵢ` are the dictionary and being [[overcompleteness|overcomplete]] means having more of them than dimensions. Stated formally, **superposition is a dictionary learning problem**, and that is the pivot the whole paper turns on.

It also carries a specific difficulty worth naming. Given the dictionary, recovering which features produced a particular activation means solving for a long vector from a short one, and infinitely many answers fit. The only thing that singles one out is insisting the answer be sparse — and finding the sparsest answer exactly is NP-hard. This is [[compressed-sensing]]: sparse structure is easy to store in a small space and genuinely hard to recover.

The tool used here is a [[sparse-autoencoder]], and it is modest by design. It reads the 512 activations, encodes them into a much wider layer through a linear map and a ReLU — 4,096 units in the run studied most closely, up to 131,072 in the largest — then decodes back to 512 and tries to reproduce what it read. It is trained on squared reconstruction error plus an [[l1-coefficient|L1 penalty]] on the hidden activations, the standard tractable stand-in for “use as few units as possible”.

The hidden units are the candidate features: each one's [[feature-direction|direction]] is a column of the decoder, its [[feature-activation|activation]] is how strongly it fired.

Two choices matter more than they look.

The reconstruction loss is squared error, not cross-entropy — which is not incidental, given the previous section. Had it been trained the way the language model was, the decomposition would have had the same incentive to blur, and you would get [[superposition-all-the-way-down]].

And the tool is weak on purpose. Better dictionary learning algorithms exist, and the worry about them is precise: the transformer is certainly not solving an NP-hard recovery problem when it reads its own activations downstream. An algorithm cleverer than the model could extract structure the model cannot use, leaving you with a confident account of something that is not happening. A sparse autoencoder is architecturally an MLP layer, which is a fair ceiling on what the model can do to itself.

beats.heading: How you know the features were not invented
beats.body:
This is the question everything turns on, and the answer is the most satisfying thing in the paper.

A [[sparse-autoencoder]] always returns something. Ask for 4,096 features and you get 4,096, whether or not the model has anything of the kind. Worse, activations reflect two things at once: what the model computes, and what the data was like. Correlations in [[pile-dataset|the Pile]] can survive the first half of the model untouched, so the features could in principle be facts about the text wearing a costume.

Here is what rules that out. **The autoencoder only ever sees MLP activations.** It never sees the [[mlp-output-weights|output matrix]] that carries them back to the residual stream, never sees the [[unembedding-matrix|unembedding]], never sees the loss, never sees a single predicted token. Half the model is hidden from it.

So take a feature it found and go looking in the half it never saw. In a one-layer model the path from MLP to logits is nearly linear, so a feature's effect on every vocabulary token — its [[logit-weight|logit weights]] — is one matrix product, computable in closed form with no experiment at all. You can also [[feature-ablation|ablate the feature]] from a real forward pass and record which predictions get worse. And you can [[pinned-feature-sampling|clamp it to a high value]] and sample.

If a feature found by reconstructing inputs turns out to have a coherent, matching effect on outputs, that agreement is not something the fitting could have manufactured. **The thing being predicted was never fit.**

That is the shape of the whole existence proof: fit on the input side, validate on the output side.

beats.heading: One feature, followed all the way through
beats.body:
Take `A/1/3450`, [[arabic-script-feature|the feature that fires on Arabic script]], through the [[feature-evidence-template|five claims]] the paper makes about each feature it studies closely.

**[[activation-specificity|Specificity]].** Testing this at scale needs a mechanical judge, so the authors build a [[computational-proxy|computational proxy]] — a log-likelihood ratio scoring how much more likely a string is under “this is Arabic” than under the data distribution generally, which is tractable because Arabic script occupies known Unicode blocks. Over 40 million tokens: Arabic is 0.13% of the data, but **81%** of where this feature is active, and **98%** where its activation exceeds 5. It gets muddier at the faint end, and the authors give [[weak-activation-hypotheses|three candidate explanations]] without choosing between them.

**[[activation-sensitivity|Sensitivity]].** It misses the definite article ال — where a different Arabic feature fires instead. Several features share the work, split partly along the seams of [[utf8-multi-token-characters|characters that tokenise into two pieces]], one feature taking the first byte and another the last. Alone it correlates **0.74** with the proxy.

**[[feature-downstream-effects|Downstream effect]].** Three independent tests agree. Its logit weights are bimodal — a large mode at zero and a small distant one containing Arabic characters and, specifically, `\xd8` and `\xd9`, the leading bytes of most UTF-8 Arabic codepoints. Ablating it hurts every Arabic prediction and helps a period, the one character shared with other scripts. And clamped high after a prompt counting to ten, the model writes Arabic.

**[[feature-neuron-nonalignment|Not a neuron]].** Search all 512 neurons' top-20 examples for Arabic and exactly one turns up, with a single instance. Write the feature's direction in [[neuron-basis-coefficients|the neuron basis]] and its three largest coefficients are all *negative*, with 27 neurons above 0.1 in magnitude. The [[most-correlated-neuron|most correlated neuron]] responds to a mixture of non-English languages with Arabic a sliver.

That last point has a detail the paper states twice without joining up. The neuron most correlated with the Arabic feature and the neuron most correlated with the [[hebrew-feature]] are the same neuron, `A/neurons/489`. Two distinct, causally confirmed features, both faint shadows on one shared axis, [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis|neither visible in it]]. Languages are close to mutually exclusive in text, which makes them ideal to place in superposition together — so that is exactly where you would expect to find them.

**[[universality|Universality]].** Train a second transformer from a different seed, learn a second dictionary, and the matching feature returns at **0.91** activation correlation. Same for the [[dna-feature|DNA feature]] at 0.92 and the [[base64-feature|base64 feature]] at 0.85.

beats.heading: Whether the typical feature is like that one
beats.body:
Four features chosen for being easy to write a proxy for prove that clean features exist. They do not prove the other four thousand are.

[[manual-interpretability-scoring|A blinded annotator scored]] features and neurons on a rubric out of 14, with one precaution that matters. Reading only a unit's top examples is how this analysis usually flatters itself — plenty of polysemantic neurons look clean at the top and reveal themselves further down. So the activation range was cut into eleven bands and sampled evenly. The **median neuron scored 0**, meaning no hypothesis could be formed at all. The **median feature interval scored 12**.

Then mechanically. [[automated-interpretability|Have Claude write an explanation]] of a feature from where it fires, then have a fresh copy use only that explanation to predict activations on unseen tokens, with no leakage. Features are predicted substantially better than neurons.

The sharper version of that test is the best single number in the paper. Take the explanation written from *activations*, and ask whether it predicts [[automated-logit-scoring|what the feature makes more likely to come next]]. Two different halves of the model, joined by nothing but the hypothesis. Chance is 50%; **neurons score 58%; features score 74%**.

The control that closes the loop: shuffle the entries within each of the trained transformer's weight matrices, preserving every weight distribution exactly and destroying only the structure, then [[randomized-transformer|run the whole procedure again]]. What comes back is a pile of single-token features and, beyond those, nothing interpretable. The data supplies the trivial structure; everything else came from training.

And coverage: splicing the autoencoder's reconstruction in place of the real activations, [[loss-recovered-by-features|79% of the MLP's loss contribution survives]] in the main run and 94.5% in the largest. The authors supply the caveat themselves — the yardstick is deleting the MLP entirely, which is a generous baseline.

beats.heading: Ask for more features and they split
beats.body:
The paper's second idea, and the one that changes how the method is used.

Features arrive in families. 512 dictionary entries give one [[base64-feature]]; 4,096 give three; 16,384 give more. This is [[feature-splitting]], and the proposed reading is that [[dictionary-learning]] never *drops* a feature when the budget is tight — it returns one covering roughly the same territory, less specifically. Widen the budget and it separates. Run UMAP over the directions from several runs and the families are geometric, not just semantic: similar features sit at small angles to each other.

Which makes dictionary size a resolution setting rather than a number you must guess right. Too few features gives a blurry picture, not a wrong one.

The three-way base64 split is worth following for what falls out. One fires on letters, one on digits, and their logit weights are nearly identical but for one systematic difference: the digit feature is markedly less inclined to predict digits. That looks arbitrary until you remember [[byte-pair-encoding|how the tokenizer works]] — two adjacent digits would have been merged into a single token, so `[Bq][8][9][mp]` never occurs. A lone digit token is therefore genuine evidence that the next token is not a digit, even inside a uniformly random base64 string. The model learned a fact about its own tokenizer and built a feature on it, one of several such [[tokenization-artifacts-in-features|artifacts surfacing as structure]].

The third feature has no obvious rule until you notice it responds to base64 that *decodes to printable ASCII*, as against base64 encoding arbitrary binary. The tell was the token `ICAgICAg`, which decodes to six spaces.

Sit with that. The model does not merely have a base64 feature; it distinguishes base64 carrying text from base64 carrying anything else. Nobody would have gone looking for it — which is the argument for finding features bottom-up rather than hypothesising them and hunting.

Features also chain, [[finite-state-automata-features|though not through weights]]. One raises the probability of certain tokens; one is sampled; that token switches on the next feature. Four of them form a loop emitting valid HTML — open tag, tag name, close, whitespace, open again. A longer chain memorises the licence boilerplate at the top of millions of source files. All inside one MLP layer, 512 neurons wide.

beats.heading: What this does not settle
beats.body:
Stated plainly, mostly by the authors.

It is [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|one layer]], and the choice cuts both ways. Because the MLP output reaches the logits almost linearly, features are more likely to be linear here *and* every check in the paper was cheap to run — which is exactly why the result may not transfer to a deep model. Others have since found interpretable features in multi-layer models, which helps.

It covers the MLP only. Attention has the same reasons to be in superposition and no demonstrated treatment; the authors flag it as a likely future bottleneck.

Nobody knows how much is left. Widening the dictionary keeps turning up [[feature-density|rarer features]] with no sign of saturation — 512 neurons were still yielding new ones at 131,072 dictionary entries. There is also an [[ultralow-density-cluster|ultralow density cluster]] of features that fire almost never and mean nothing, an artifact of the training procedure, reproduced independently, cause still unknown.

Interpretability degrades at the bottom of the activation spectrum, and it is unresolved whether that is proxy error, genuine model uncertainty, or learned directions sitting at a slight angle to the true ones.

And there is still [[evaluating-dictionary-learning|no reliable way to tell a good dictionary from a bad one]]. That is the central methodological gap: the sparsity coefficient and the dictionary size are set by proxies and judgement. Scaling is a serious engineering problem on top — a 100× autoencoder on a single 10,000-wide MLP layer runs to roughly 20 billion parameters, and rare features may demand training on a large fraction of the base model's own corpus.

What is left is this. The plan was to break the model into components, understand each, and compose upward. The components are not the ones the architecture hands you. They are a larger, sparser set of directions, and you can recover them with a small autoencoder trained to reconstruct what the layer was already doing — then check your work in the half of the model that autoencoder never saw.

That is not an understanding of a language model. It is the thing you needed before you could start.
